Empirical Research Plan: “How does the extension of unemployment-insurance (UI) benefits affect unemployment duration and re-employment outcomes in Germany, and does the effect depend on aggregate labour-market conditions?”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Primary design: Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD), supplemented by a “difference-in-discontinuities” (DiDisc) specification.

Why RDD?  
• The 1980s reform lengthened entitlement only for job-seekers whose age at the start of a spell exceeded a statutory cut-off (e.g. 45 or 50).  
• Age is continuous and impossible to manipulate in practice (reported on social-security records).  
• Benefit duration jumps discretely at the cut-off, whereas potential outcomes in the absence of the reform are assumed to be smooth in age.  
• Because the rule became effective on a known date, we can difference out any pre-existing age-related discontinuity by comparing cohorts starting spells just before vs. just after the reform (DiDisc = RD × DID).

Economy-state heterogeneity: Interact the RD treatment indicator with the contemporaneous local unemployment rate (or national cycle dummy) in the second stage.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Running variable: Agei  = precise age in days at the *start* of spell i.  
Cut-off: a0  = 45.000 years (16,436 days).  
Treatment indicator (first stage): Zi = 1{Agei ≥ a0 & spell starts on/after 1 July 1988}.

• Treated observations: Unemployed entrants within a bandwidth h around a0, whose age ≥ a0 after the reform (they are *eligible* for, and overwhelmingly receive, longer UI).  
• Control observations: Entrants in the same age window but < a0.  
• Fuzzy RD: Some < a0 may still draw long benefits (early retirement rules, disability), and some ≥ a0 may exit UI early, so treatment is measured as “potential benefit duration” (PBD).  The jump in PBD at a0 is the first stage; we instrument actual weeks-of-UI received (Di) with Zi.

Timing: Index time in *days since reform*; only spells that start within, say, ±24 months of 1 July 1988 enter the main estimation window.

Outcome variables:  
 Y1i  = unemployment duration (weeks).  
 Y2i  = log re-employment wage.  

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Continuity of counterfactual outcome in age.  
Plausible because nothing but entitlement changes exactly at 45.

A2. No precise manipulation of age at spell start.  
Highly credible: date of birth is administratively verified.

A3. First-stage relevance: jump in potential benefit duration at cutoff.  
Documented legislatively; can be verified in data.

A4. Stable unit treatment value / no spillovers within narrow bandwidth.  
UI schedule depends only on own age.

A5 (for DiDisc supplement). Any age-specific discontinuity is constant over the short pre-/post-reform window (“parallel discontinuities”).  
Short horizon makes this plausible; testable with pre-trend checks.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Age-specific labour-market shocks unrelated to UI.  
→ Use DiDisc (subtract pre-reform difference).  
→ Control flexibly for age × year trends outside the local window.

T2. Sorting of spell *start dates* relative to birthday (“timing into unemployment”).  
→ Plot density of running variable separately pre- and post-reform (McCrary test).  
→ Narrow ±6-month window and show robustness to even tighter windows.

T3. Differential enforcement/administration by local agencies.  
→ Add local-office fixed effects.  
→ Cluster standard errors at the agency × entry-month level.  
→ Show robustness excluding regions with atypical enforcement.

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
###############################################################################
# 0. Packages
###############################################################################
library(data.table)      # fast data handling
library(fixest)          # regressions with high-dim FE
library(rdrobust)        # local-linear RD
library(sandwich); library(lmtest)

###############################################################################
# 1. Load and prepare data
###############################################################################
ui <- fread("german_UI_1980_2004.csv")

# Reform date
ref_date <- as.Date("1988-07-01")

# Running variable: age in days at spell start
ui[, age_days := as.numeric(start_date - birth_date)]
ui[, age_yrs  := age_days/365.25]

# Post-reform indicator
ui[, post := as.integer(start_date >= ref_date)]

# Eligibility jump (instrument)
cutoff_days <- 45*365.25
ui[, Z := as.integer(post==1 & age_days >= cutoff_days)]

# Potential benefit duration (weeks) – already in data or constructed
# ui[, pbd_weeks := ...]   # first stage var

# Treatment (actual weeks of UI received)
# ui[, ui_weeks := ...]    # outcome of first stage

# Outcomes
# ui[, unemp_weeks := ...]
# ui[, log_rwage   := log(reemployment_wage)]

# Bandwidth h (initial)
h <- 5*365.25  # ±5 years; will be tightened later
sample <- ui[abs(age_days - cutoff_days) <= h &
             start_date %between% c(ref_date - 365*2, ref_date + 365*2)]

###############################################################################
# 2. Fuzzy RD (two-stage) using fixest
###############################################################################
# First stage: jump in potential benefit duration
fs <- feols(pbd_weeks ~ Z | 0 | 0 | agency_id, data = sample)
summary(fs)

# Second stage: unemployment duration
rd_main <- feols(unemp_weeks ~ 1 | 0 | (ui_weeks ~ Z) | agency_id,
                 data = sample)
summary(rd_main)

# Heterogeneity by local unemployment rate (lo_ur)
rd_het <- feols(unemp_weeks ~ lo_ur | 0 | (ui_weeks ~ Z + Z:lo_ur) |
                agency_id, data = sample)
summary(rd_het)

###############################################################################
# 3. Non-parametric check with rdrobust
###############################################################################
rdrobust(sample$unemp_weeks, sample$age_days - cutoff_days,
         c = 0, fuzzy = sample$Z)

###############################################################################
# 4. Robustness: placebo cut-off at 43
###############################################################################
placebo <- sample
placebo[, placebo_run := age_days - 43*365.25]
rdrobust(placebo$unemp_weeks, placebo$placebo_run, c = 0, fuzzy = placebo$Z)

###############################################################################
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Theory (moral-hazard framework) predicts that longer UI prolongs search, *especially* when aggregate unemployment is low (outside options good). I expect:

• Elasticity of unemployment duration w.r.t. potential benefit duration ≈ 0.2.  
– A 6-month (≈26-week) extension should raise average spell length by ≈5 weeks (about 20 %).  
• Re-employment wages may rise slightly (≈1–2 %) if longer search improves match quality, but the sign is ambiguous.

During high-unemployment years the effect on duration should be weaker (congested labour market lowers marginal utility of extra search time).

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1. Clear discontinuity in treatment at cutoff ………………… 1  
C2. Running variable not manipulable …………………………… 1  
C3. Smoothness of baseline covariates at cutoff ……………… 1 (to be verified)  
C4. Robust to bandwidth and polynomial choice ……………… 0.5 (to be checked)  
C5. No other simultaneous policy change at cutoff ………… 1  

Total = 4.5 / 5 → strong but still requires robustness work.

────────────────────────────────────────
End of plan
